analysis.title: The Myth Of AI's Miracle: Albert Edwards Spots The Same Fatal Flaw That Sank Asia In 1997
key_insights: SocGen's Albert Edwards compares the AI boom to the 1990s East Asian Miracle. His trigger is subdued total factor productivity (TFP) growth, the same statistic Krugman used in 1994 to argue Asia's growth came from capital and labor accumulation, not efficiency.

Apollo's Torsten Slok shows utilization-adjusted TFP from the San Francisco Fed slightly below zero with no acceleration since the AI capex cycle began, while output per hour runs near 2.5%. Slok calls this the signature of capital deepening, not a technology shock.
Edwards says the flaw exposed in Asia was that investors lent cheap, abundant capital that was misallocated, which showed up as poor TFP growth. He applies the same logic to AI funding.

Net business investment (Parenteau chart) is flat after proper depreciation. Real gross investment is a record ~15.5% of GDP, but real net is flat near 3.5%, about where it was in 2015 and 2019. Nominal gross is ~14% of GDP and nominal net has been around 3% for a decade (both read off charts, approximate).
Business fixed investment adds well under 1 percentage point to annual US GDP growth, versus a peak above 2 points in the late 1990s.

Equipment investment grows ~14% y/y nominal but 'barely double digits' in real terms, so part of the AI boom in GDP accounts is price, not volume. Non-residential structures are contracting, about -3% nominal and -6% real, despite the datacenter rollout.
Goldman estimates global AI investment will exceed $1 trillion in 2026, with the US and Canada about 60% of net data center capacity additions.

Goldman's internet team splits the buildout into three phases: ~$633B over 2023-25, ~$1.73T over 2026-27 and ~$4.14T over 2028-30. A 15% ROIC on Phase 2 requires the six US hyperscalers to earn ~$1.42T of cumulative revenue over 2028-30. Annual spend rises from ~$211B to ~$1.38T, a 6.5x increase.
In Goldman's worst case where hyperscaler ROIC on capex is zero, the hyperscalers still need ~$920B of annual revenue to cover depreciation and running costs.

The article argues the closer Asian analogy is the funding source. The bond bear market continues, France has been the focus (worst decade for French bonds since 1803 per the author), and Edwards says the bond vigilantes may move next to Japan, the UK or the US. AI issuers (Broadcom, Oracle, SpaceX) are adding debt that needs the same duration buyers.

The Nasdaq fell more than 1% after the FT reported OpenAI's annualized revenue is about $20B below what was previously signaled. The article cites roughly $50B annualized revenue against $1.5T of commitments.

The 10Y Treasury yield hit 5.36% this week, described as a multi-decade high. The Fed hiked in September for the first time since July 2023, under Chair Warsh, despite his thesis that AI is deflationary. The S&P 500 is at a record high.

Counterpoint: Edwards concedes it may be too early for AI to show up in TFP. Slok notes electricity and IT each took a decade or more to show in aggregate numbers. Goldman's Briggs would call this the early innings of a general-purpose technology.

sector_views.rationale: Edwards is skeptical of the AI boom as a bubble with misallocated cheap capital and no visible TFP payoff. He does not declare it dead.

macro_indicators.interpretation: No sign of AI-driven productivity acceleration since the capex cycle began.
Strong output per hour with flat TFP points to capital deepening, not a technology shock.
Described as a multi-decade high. Competes with AI-related debt issuance for funding.
Record share, but real net investment after depreciation is flat near 3.5%.

macro_indicators.reading: ~14% y/y nominal, barely double digits real
macro_indicators.interpretation: Part of the growth is price rather than volume.

macro_indicators.reading: Rate hike in September 2026, first since July 2023
macro_indicators.interpretation: Fed is not setting policy on an AI productivity forecast and is concerned about AI-related inflation.

risk_factors: AI buildout financed by cheap debt (investment-grade bonds, private credit, SPVs) that needs duration buyers while the bond bear market continues.
Bond vigilantes rolling from France to Japan, the UK or the US.
Depreciation risk from lengthening GPU useful-life schedules, which flatters gross investment and earnings (Burry's critique).
Revenue shortfall against commitments: OpenAI at roughly $50B annualized revenue versus $1.5T of commitments.
Memory chip and equipment price inflation making AI spending look larger in nominal terms than in real terms.
Troubled Firmus IPO shows what happens when equity is worth less than debt.
charts_described: Slok chart: utilization-adjusted TFP from the San Francisco Fed slightly below zero versus output per hour near 2.5%.
Parenteau chart: nominal gross business investment ~14% of GDP and net ~3% for a decade. Real gross ~15.5% of GDP and real net ~3.5%.
Edwards chart: contribution of US business fixed investment to y/y GDP growth, well under 1 point versus above 2 points in the late 1990s.
vol_and_positioning: The Nasdaq fell more than 1% on the FT report that OpenAI's annualized revenue is about $20B less than previously signaled, while the S&P 500 sits at a record high.
cross_bank_references: Last month BofA's Michael Hartnett flagged the same TFP pattern, with TFP tracking consumer sentiment for half a century and both rolling over.
Edwards cites Apollo's Torsten Slok on TFP and says Slok, like many, thinks it is too early for AI to show up in TFP.
Goldman's Acemoglu vs Briggs debate from June 2024: Acemoglu 0.5% productivity and 0.9% cumulative GDP over a decade, Briggs 9% productivity and 6.1% extra GDP.
A JPM trader argued yesterday that the 1997 analogue points to a peak in bond yields.

tension_points.bull_case: Slok notes electricity and IT each took a decade or more to show up in aggregate numbers, and Goldman's Briggs sees a 9% productivity boost and 6.1% extra GDP, so the TFP lag is normal for an early-stage general-purpose technology.
tension_points.bear_case: TFP is flat to negative while output per hour is strong, which marks capital deepening. Net investment is flat after depreciation, and Edwards sees a replay of the 1993 Krugman thesis and the Asian crisis.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Visible acceleration in TFP or productivity statistics would weaken the bear case. Funding stress in bond markets or revenue shortfalls such as OpenAI's would support it.

tension_points.theme: AI debt funding and bond yields
tension_points.bull_case: A JPM trader argued the 1997 analogue points to a peak in bond yields, which would ease funding for AI issuers.
tension_points.bear_case: Bond vigilantes are rotating across markets, the 10Y is at 5.36%, and the AI complex needs duration buyers to absorb hundreds of billions of new debt.
